## Chapter 1

CHAPTER X

POLITICAL MORALITY (1862)

On Moran's promotion, Mr. Seward inquired whether Minister Adams would like the place of Assistant Secretary for his son. It was the first—and last—office ever offered him. Any young man could make some sort of Assistant Secretary; only one could make an Assistant Son. As the years went on, he found advantages in having no position at all. It lent itself to a sort of irregular education that seemed to be the only sort he was ever to get.

Under the stimulus of danger, Secretary Seward sent over every important American on whom he could lay his hands. Most interesting was Thurlow Weed, who took charge of the press. Weed was a complete American education in himself: mind naturally strong and beautifully balanced, manners perfect in the style of benevolent simplicity, the tradition of Benjamin Franklin. The trait that astounded cynicism was his apparent unselfishness. He grasped power, but not office; distributed offices by handfuls without caring to take them. Once, when Weed had told stories strong even for the Albany lobby, the private secretary asked outright: "Then, Mr. Weed, do you think that no politician can be trusted?" Weed hesitated, then said in his mild manner: "I never advise a young man to begin by thinking so."

William M. Evarts came over at the same time as law counsel. Evarts was as individual as Weed was impersonal; an economist of morals, with him the question was rather how much morality one could afford. "The world can absorb only doses of truth," he said; "too much would kill it." One sought education in order to adjust the dose.

England's power of absorbing truth was small. Englishmen like Palmerston, Russell, Bethell offered a study that sickened a young student with anxiety. Was their bad faith to be taken for granted? Life changed front, according as one thought one's self dealing with honest men or with rogues.

The recognition of belligerency, the Declaration of Paris, the Trent Affair—all strengthened the belief that Lord Russell had started in May, 1861, with the assumption that the Confederacy was established. With the insolence of youth, Henry Adams jumped to the conclusion that Earl Russell lied. The most costly tutors in the world were provided for him at public expense—Palmerston, Russell, Westbury, Gladstone, Granville on one side; Seward, Charles Francis Adams, Evarts, Weed on the other—but there was only one student to profit by this immense staff.

The demonstration began in June, 1862. After the escape of one rebel cruiser, Adams remonstrated against the imminent escape of "No. 290." Lord Russell declined to act. On July 24, Collier's legal opinion declared it "difficult to make out a stronger case of infringement of the Foreign Enlistment Act, which, if not enforced, is little better than a dead letter." Four days afterwards, Earl Russell let the ship escape. If one could not trust a dozen of the most respected private characters in the world, composing the Queen's Ministry, one could trust no mortal man.

Russell felt the force of this inference and undertook to disprove it. The effort lasted till his death. Minister Adams held the convenient belief that Russell was true, and the theory answered his purposes so well that he died still holding it. His son was older than his father in 1862. The most curious fact was that Russell believed in his own good faith, and Argyll believed in it also.

The *Alabama* escaped, by Russell's confessed negligence, on July 28, 1862. After the Union disasters before Richmond and at Bull Run, and Lee's invasion of Maryland, Palmerston wrote Russell on September 14: "If this should happen, would it not be time for us to consider whether England and France might not address the contending parties and recommend an arrangement on the basis of separation?"

Forty years later, Gladstone's own confession revealed that the Cabinet's drift toward intervention had been even nearer success than Adams had supposed; the lesson stood, that in politics no professed friend in power could be trusted, and that the diplomatic victory of 1862 had been won against men who scarcely knew their own minds.
